query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In equiatomic single‐phase CrFeCoNiX HEAs, an alloy with X = Al (at or above a threshold Al content) will form and sustain a thin, coherent protective oxide layer (predominantly Al2O3) during exposure at >900 °C, whereas alloys with X = Mn or Si will develop thicker, porous oxides that crack or spall.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic single‐phase CrFeCoNiX high‐entropy alloy synthesized via arc melting, with controlled variation: one alloy containing high Al, one with Mn, and one with Si as the X element.
generation.intervention: Expose each alloy to oxidizing conditions at temperatures exceeding 900 °C (e.g., 900–1050 °C) for 24 hours.
generation.conditions: Air (or defined corrosive atmosphere) under isothermal conditions at >900 °C for 24 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a nanoscale, continuous oxide scale; specifically, a coherent Al2O3 layer in the Al–alloy vs. discontinuous, porous Mn- or Si-based oxide scales.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum’s lower diffusion rate and stronger thermodynamic drive (lower Gibbs free energy of oxide formation) favor the nucleation and growth of a protective, adherent Al2O3 scale, whereas Mn (with high mobility) and Si lead to volatile or non‐coherent oxide structures that crack under thermal stresses.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al-containing alloy will exhibit an oxide layer approximately 1 μm thick that remains adherent and protective, while the Mn- and Si-containing alloys will form oxide layers exceeding 5–10 μm that show significant porosity, cracking, and spallation relative to a baseline alloy lacking significant X content.
generation.baseline: Control alloy without a significant addition of Al (or with low Al content), which typically forms non‑protective, multi‑component oxide scales under the same conditions.
generation.boundary: Applicable to alloys in a single-phase metallic solid-solution state; exposure at temperatures >900 °C in an oxidizing or corrosive atmosphere.
generation.uncertainty: Potential interactions with minor impurities or secondary phases that may modify local diffusion kinetics; threshold Al concentration effects may vary with processing history.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of equiatomic CrFeCoNiX alloys with X = Al, Mn, and Si. Expose samples to air at 950 °C for 24 hours. Use cross-sectional TEM and XRD to characterize oxide scale thickness, composition, and adherence.
measurements: Adhesion quality (using scratch tests and microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing alloy does not form a significantly thinner, coherent oxide scale relative to the Mn and Si variants—or if unexpectedly stable oxide layers form in the Mn or Si alloys—the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: At temperatures exceeding 500 °C, the oxidation behavior of traditional and complex alloys (e.g., Ni-Cr, Ni-based superalloys, Fe-Cr, CoCrFeNiMn ‘Cantor’ alloy) has been extensively studied in oxygen-rich environments and over extended periods (from days to hundreds of days,). Key contributors to the process include species transport to the oxide/metal junction within the base alloy, movement across the oxide/metal interface, and passage through the oxide layer. For instance, atmospheric oxidation of CoCrFeNiMn-containing alloys results in a layered oxide film, with Cr-rich inner and Mn-rich outer oxides attributed to outward cation diffusion. In a study by Kim et al., the high-temperature oxidation of FeCrMnNiCo (900–1100 °C in 20% O2/80% N2 for 24 h) showed the formation of layered Cr2O3 and Mn2O3 oxides at 900 °C. This process led to Ni, Fe, and Co enrichment in the base alloy. At 1000–1100 °C, the outer Mn2O3 layer changed to Mn3O4, forming a (Mn, Cr)3O4 ternary oxide with Ni, Fe, and Co in a solid solution. cited_evidence.text: In the case of the Mn15Al5 alloy, the outer part of the oxide layer was mainly composed of Mn, suggesting the presence of MnxOy oxides followed by a thin layer of Cr-based oxides found at the metal/oxide interface. Moreover, a significant level of porosity was found within its closest proximity of it. The overall thickness of the whole layer after 100 h annealing reached approximately 25 µm. More importantly, the Mn15Al5 alloy was the only one showing strong sub-surface oxidation and developed internal porosity due to the diffusion of Mn toward the oxide layer. It was found that the sub-surface porosity reached up to ≈100 µm into the alloy core and likely may further progress with the increasing time of annealing. The present oxides within the metal were mainly composed of Mn and Al. Increasing the content of Al above 5 at.% resulted in a completely different behavior, forming a well-protective oxide layer containing foremostly Al, suggesting the formation of AlxOy without any traces of chipping or formation of sub-surface oxides. papers.title: Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys.
papers.system: Multi‐element high-entropy alloys (e.g., CoCrFeNiMn and variants with additions such as Al)
papers.approach: In situ atom probe tomography, high-resolution electron microscopy, XANES, and oxidation tests under controlled oxygen exposure
papers.findings: Observed layered oxide films with an inner, Cr-rich (and sometimes Al‐rich) zone and an outer region enriched in more mobile elements (e.g., Mn). The results highlight that element-specific diffusion rates and redox properties dictate the oxidation sequence and the eventual coherence of the oxide layer.
papers.mechanism: The preferential interactivity parameter (PIP) based on standard reduction potentials, atomic radii, and cohesive energy density guides which element migrates to the surface first; faster-diffusing elements (like Mn) form volatile/non-protective oxides while slower diffusing ones (Cr, Al) can form stable protective oxides when present in sufficient quantity.

papers.title: Thermodynamic Insights into the Oxidation Mechanisms of CrMnFeCoNi High-Entropy Alloy Using In Situ X-ray Diffraction.
papers.approach: In situ high-temperature XRD coupled with thermodynamic calculations (CALPHAD/ThermoCalc) during exposure to air and vacuum at temperatures reaching 1100 °C
papers.findings: Revealed that at high temperatures (above ~900 °C), manganese-dominated oxidation leads to non-protective, multi-layered oxide scales where volatile phases or spinel oxides form. The expected protective Cr2O3 is not clearly observed, with degradation linked to Mn depletion.
papers.mechanism: Differences in element mobility (Mn > Cr > Fe > Co > Ni) and the volatility of Cr oxide (CrO3 formation at high temperatures) govern the inability to form a coherent protective layer. Instead, oxide layers evolve into a graded structure that is subject to spallation.

papers.title: Influence of the Al Content on the Properties of Mechanically Alloyed CoCrFeNiMnXAl20-X High-Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: Mechanically alloyed CoCrFeNiMnXAl(20-X) HEAs (varying X = Mn with partial substitution by Al)
papers.approach: Mechanical alloying and subsequent oxidation tests comparing samples with different Al contents under prolonged high-temperature exposure
papers.findings: Higher Al content alloys formed thin, coherent and protective Al-based oxide scales (AlxOy), while lower Al content resulted in thick, porous oxide layers dominated by Mn oxides that exhibited extensive subsurface oxidation and porosity.
papers.mechanism: Aluminum, with its lower oxide growth rate and higher thermodynamic stability (favoring Al2O3 formation), retards further oxidation if present above a threshold concentration. In contrast, when Al is low, the more mobile Mn leads to unstable oxide formation.

papers.title: Modeling Oxidation of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Using Stochastic Cellular Automata.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (single-crystal and dendritic microstructures)
papers.approach: Stochastic cellular automata simulations based on diffusion coefficients from molecular simulations, informed by experimental microstructures
papers.findings: Simulations revealed that in a single-phase, homogeneous microstructure, oxide formation yields predominantly α-Al2O3 and Cr2O3 scales with parabolic kinetics. In multiphase (dendritic vs interdendritic) systems, segregation leads to spatially distinct oxide regimes, though overall oxidation kinetics remain similar.
papers.mechanism: The interplay of bulk and grain-boundary diffusion controls the spatial distribution and thickness of oxide scales. Protective oxides form in regions with higher local Al and Cr concentrations, whereas zones with enrichment of more mobile elements demonstrate less protective behavior.

papers.title: Enhanced Oxidation Resistance of Ultrafine-Grain Microstructure AlCoCrFeNi High Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with ultrafine-grained versus as-cast microstructures
papers.approach: Experimental studies utilizing controlled oxidation tests, cross-sectional microscopy, and kinetic analysis over temperature ranges between 900–1050 °C
papers.findings: Ultrafine-grained microstructures, with a high density of grain boundaries, facilitate rapid formation of a coherent, Cr-rich protective oxide scale that limits further oxidation. In contrast, coarser-grained (as-cast) alloys produce non-adherent, mixed oxide scales prone to spallation.
papers.mechanism: The enhanced grain boundary diffusion in ultrafine-grained samples promotes the fast establishment of a continuous protective chromium oxide layer, which acts as a diffusion barrier against oxygen ingress.

papers.title: High Temperature Oxidation Behavior of an Equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.approach: 3D laser printing produced samples; oxidation experiments at 700 °C and 900 °C with phase identification via XRD and microstructural analysis
papers.findings: At 900 °C, the alloy develops an unstable, multi-component oxide scale (including MnFe2O4, MnFeO2, and Cr2O3) that spalls off and fails to act as an effective barrier, in contrast to behavior observed at lower temperatures (700 °C) where oxides are less prone to cracking.
papers.mechanism: A competition between rapid diffusion of Mn (and other elements) and insufficient formation of a coherent, continuous Cr-rich layer leads to a scale that cannot accommodate thermal stresses, resulting in cracking and spallation.

established: High-temperature oxidation (>900 °C) in HEAs is strongly influenced by the relative diffusion rates and redox potentials of constituent elements.
Protective oxide layers (e.g., Cr2O3, Al2O3) can form if elements with slower diffusion and lower volatility are present in adequate concentration.
Microstructural features (e.g., grain size, phase homogeneity) play a critical role in determining oxide scale coherence and integrity.

approaches_tried.approach: In situ characterization (AP, HTXRD) to monitor oxide phase evolution under elevated temperatures
approaches_tried.outcome: Successful identification of layered structures and phase transitions, though discrepancies in the formation of expected protective oxides (e.g., Cr2O3) were noted.

approaches_tried.approach: Stochastic cellular automata simulations based on diffusion coefficients for different alloying elements
approaches_tried.outcome: Provided mesoscale insights into oxide layer formation and evolution across homogeneous and multiphase microstructures.

approaches_tried.approach: Controlled alloying with increased Al content
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated that alloys with higher Al content form thinner, coherent, and protective oxide scales in contrast to Mn-dominated, porous scales in low-Al variants.

mechanisms: Differential element diffusion: Faster-diffusing elements (e.g., Mn) lead to non-protective, volatile oxides, while slower-diffusing elements (Cr, Al) can form stable scales.
Thermodynamic stability: Elements with more negative Gibbs free energies (e.g., Al for Al2O3) preferentially form protective oxides.
Microstructural effects: Grain size and phase distribution influence diffusion pathways and the integrity of the oxide scale.
disagreements: Some studies (e.g., in situ HTXRD) did not observe expected formation of protective Cr2O3 at high temperatures, whereas modeling and thermodynamic predictions sometimes indicate its presence.

Variability in oxide scale formation: While certain processing routes and alloying additions promote coherent oxide layers, other reports show spallation and cracking even in similar compositional systems.
open_questions: How do different X additions (Si vs. Mn vs. Al) in CrFeCoNiX specifically tune the diffusion kinetics and redox behavior that govern oxide layer stability above 900 °C?
What is the influence of single-phase versus multiphase metallic solid-solution states on the development and adherence of protective oxide scales under oxidative versus corrosive atmospheres?
Under what precise environmental and microstructural conditions can a switch be induced between stable protective oxides and unstable, spalling scales?
opportunities: Conduct a controlled comparative study of CrFeCoNiX alloys (with X = Si, Mn, or Al) under identical high-temperature (above 900 °C) oxidative and corrosive exposures to isolate the role of each additive element.
Employ advanced in situ characterization (e.g., APT, HTXRD, TEM) during oxidation to track element-specific diffusion pathways and oxide layer evolution in both single- and multiphase states.

Investigate the combined effect of controlled alloying and microstructural engineering (e.g., grain refinement, phase homogeneity) to optimize the conditions under which a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists.

directions.direction: Investigate the effect of the X element (Si, Mn, or Al) on oxide scale formation via composition design.
directions.assessment: This direction directly targets the role of alloying additions in controlling oxidation. Prior evidence shows that high Al content promotes formation of protective Al2O3 scales while Mn leads to volatile or non‐protective oxides. The underlying physics—including redox thermodynamics and elemental diffusion kinetics—support this approach. It is highly feasible using controlled alloy synthesis and in situ characterization.

directions.direction: Examine the role of diffusion kinetics and preferential interactivity (PIP) in controlling the sequence of oxide formation.
directions.assessment: This direction tests a mechanistic hypothesis based on measured diffusion rates and redox potentials. Prior work indicates that differential cation mobilities largely govern which oxides form first. It directly attacks the question by predicting which elements migrate and under what conditions a coherent scale can be established. It is supported by both in situ studies and modelling efforts.

directions.direction: Assess microstructure effects by comparing single‐phase versus multiphase alloys and/or ultrafine‐grained versus coarse‐grained states.
directions.assessment: Microstructure has been shown to strongly influence oxidation behavior. Evidence indicates that heterogeneous (multiphase) or ultrafine‐grained structures can affect elemental diffusion and oxide scale adherence. This approach is experimentally accessible via different processing routes (e.g., controlled cooling or severe plastic deformation) and advanced electron microscopy.

directions.direction: Utilize in situ high-temperature oxidation experiments combined with advanced characterization to directly observe oxide formation kinetics and morphology evolution.
directions.assessment: Real-time monitoring (e.g., HT-XRD, TEM, APT) provides dynamic insight into the evolution of oxide scales at >900 °C. This approach directly observes the transition from protective to spalling behavior and links kinetics with microstructural changes. It is well supported by several prior studies and can offer quantifiable, falsifiable endpoints.

directions.direction: Develop and validate a stochastic cellular automata model incorporating diffusion and redox parameters to predict oxide scale evolution.
directions.assessment: Modelling can synthesize the effects of composition, diffusion kinetics, and microstructure on oxidation. Prior work using cellular automata has captured the mesoscale evolution of oxide morphology. However, while informative, the link between simulation predictions and experimental observations must be validated, making it slightly more indirect.

candidates.hypothesis: Ultrafine-grained CrFeCoNiAl alloys will form a more continuous and adherent protective oxide scale at temperatures above 900 °C compared to their coarse-grained counterparts due to enhanced grain-boundary diffusion of passivating elements.

candidates.hypothesis: The protective behavior of oxidation in CrFeCoNiX alloys is governed by the preferential interactivity parameter (PIP); alloys with a calculated PIP above a critical threshold will form a stable, coherent protective oxide layer (rich in Cr2O3 or Al2O3) under exposure above 900 °C, while those below the threshold will exhibit unstable, spalling oxide scales.
candidates.intervention: Expose the alloy samples to an oxidative environment at 950 °C under controlled oxygen partial pressures for 24 hours.
